name: Uma Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead developers who maintain appointment booking software for a tech company. I have a master’s degree, and I check reports of double bookings before the morning meeting. I like solving a bug that saved a clinic a difficult call, but I get tired of watching staff carry the blame for a confusing screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the appointment software still needs careful developers, even if AI writes a few repeated checks. I try a tool now and then, but I want to see a real error caught before I trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m paid a normal senior developer wage and have about four months of basic expenses saved. Our clinic customers renew steadily, so a small AI change does not make me fear for this year’s rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the booking team and ask our support staff for the three complaints they hear most. In the first year, I’d continue putting 120 a month into savings as long as wages and rent stay steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel fairly calm. It is nice to think the work might change slowly enough for us to check each new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which complaint stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A patient once got two appointment reminders for different days. I spent a morning tracing the change. A missed visit costs somebody time and money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who sees your savings plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Dev knows the figure because we split the rent. We keep separate accounts, and four months is my share of basic bills, not both our wages.

say: I think **appointment software** still needs careful developers when AI writes routine checks.
I want a tool to **catch a real error** before our team trusts it.
think: I have **four months saved** and ordinary senior pay.
I expect our **clinic renewals** to keep this year’s rent secure.
do: **Keep leading** the booking team and ask support for its three main complaints.
**Save 120 monthly** while my wages and rent remain steady.
feel: **Calm** about this small change and time to check new tools.
S0.quote: A missed visit costs somebody time and money.
fieldNote: Her trust starts with **patient outcomes**, not the speed of generated code.
A **four-month cushion** and steady clinic renewals support calm here, though she keeps adding to savings while pay continues.

steps.text: Keep leading the clinic appointment booking team
Save 120 monthly while wages and rent stay steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our team to show which generated booking changes were checked by a person. I’d also ask our workplace group to push for paid training before easy coding tickets disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many checks and small fixes in my day are thinking work, so this would reach me quickly. I can review hard cases, but a smaller team might mean longer hours for the same pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask a colleague to show me how they use AI to test double bookings, then practise on our safe test system. In the first year of strong change I’d bring the workplace group a proposal for paid training and written staffing figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy about hours and whether management keeps the roster honest, though my wage still looks secure. I need proof the new method works before I trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you the tool helped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare its double-booking warnings against twenty past incidents. An AI tool that misses two clinics sharing a room cannot approve a release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your partner share the worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev works in a library and has his own hours to worry about. We would postpone a holiday before touching rent money, but we have not planned that cut yet.

say: I want **human checks** named on generated booking changes.
I want our **workplace group** to seek paid training before easy tickets disappear.
think: I expect routine **checks and fixes** in my work to change quickly.
I fear **longer hours** for the same wage if our team shrinks.
do: **Learn an AI test** for double bookings with a colleague on our safe system this month.
**Bring a proposal** for paid training and staffing figures to the workplace group.
feel: **Uneasy** about longer hours and team size, while my wage still looks secure.
S1.quote: An AI tool that misses two clinics sharing a room cannot approve a release.
fieldNote: She will learn after **peer demonstration** and compare the tool against twenty known incidents.
Her **current wage** looks secure, but she wants paid training and headcount facts before accepting longer hours.

steps.text: Practise an AI double-booking test with a colleague on the safe system
Ask the workplace group to seek paid training and staffing figures

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could build most of our booking system, and management should tell us what happens to staff. Robots in about 2031 concern clinic workers doing physical tasks, but my screen work changes in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose the senior role I spent years earning before a new job path is clear. Four months saved would go quickly if many developers apply to the same openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our workplace group this month to seek written notice and paid transition terms, and I’d pause the deposit on a larger flat with Dev. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my job ends, I’d apply for paid clinic support roles only if vacancies exist; I’d use savings for rent while looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be frightened and short of sleep. I can make a list, but two years is barely enough to find out what work still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dev about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say our current flat is small but affordable, and we should not sign a higher rent while my income is exposed. He would be disappointed, but we would decide together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid course then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Four months of expenses is rent money, not a training fund. I would take a course if the employer funded it and kept paying wages.

say: I want management to explain **staff plans** for full AGI by 2028.
I see **robots around 2031** as a later problem for physical clinic work.
think: I could lose my **senior developer role** before another path is clear.
I expect my **four-month cushion** to shrink quickly in a crowded job search.
do: **Seek written notice** and paid transition terms through our workplace group now.
**Pause the larger flat** with Dev before signing higher rent.
**Apply for paid support** only if clinic vacancies exist after a 2028 job cut, using savings for rent while looking.
feel: **Frightened** and losing sleep over a short runway.
S2.quote: Four months of expenses is rent money, not a training fund.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 screen-work shock** from robots that follow three years later.
She protects current **rent affordability** and refuses unfunded training during a job loss.

steps.text: Ask the workplace group for written notice and paid transition terms
Pause the deposit on a larger flat with Dev
Apply after 2028 job loss to paid clinic support vacancies, using savings for rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years lets clinics and developers test safer systems before full AGI arrives in 2031. I’d press the company to publish which people will check appointment mistakes after a machine writes the code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still face the thinking-work change in 2031; the robots around 2034 do not buy a developer extra years. But five years might let me build six months of savings and learn whether clinic support jobs are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d request a funded half-day each month with clinic support to learn how missed visits are handled, and take those shifts only if approved. Separately, I’d save another 80 monthly if our bills allow; after 2031 I’d apply for paid support roles only if they remain open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious but able to prepare deliberately. The written funding matters because I cannot train by quietly taking unpaid days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test a new support role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d handle real appointment calls with a support worker beside me and ask whether the department has a staffing budget. A promise that there might be work someday would not move me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the funding request is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my developer wage and ask the workplace group to raise it with management. I would not count the proposed shifts as experience I already have.

say: I want **clinic checks** named before full AGI writes the booking system in 2031.
I think five years permits **real trials** with people who handle missed visits.
think: I still face **thinking AI in 2031** despite robots coming later.
I might build **six months saved** and test whether clinic support jobs pay.
do: **Request funded clinic shifts** for half a day each month; take them only if approved.
**Save another 80 monthly** if bills allow, regardless of the clinic shift request; apply for paid support openings after 2031 if available.
feel: **Anxious but deliberate** because funded preparation could be possible.
S3.quote: I cannot train by quietly taking unpaid days.
fieldNote: Her preparation rests on **funded clinic time**, with explicit approval before any shift.
She seeks **staffing budget evidence** before treating support as a viable move.

steps.text: Take funded monthly clinic support shifts only if the company approves
Save another 80 monthly if household bills allow
Apply for paid clinic support openings if they remain after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade gives our booking team a chance to fix present problems and prepare for full AGI in 2036. I would ask workers and clinics to agree on how mistakes are reported, not just buy a new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Software might no longer buy my rent by 2036. I would be 37 then. I could reach a larger buffer and perhaps move toward patient-facing work, but that work could also change when robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep my current role and ask the clinic support team for one funded observation day each quarter. If approved, I’d attend; I’d also save toward six months of bills while wages hold, and seek paid appointment support work after 2036 only if it still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy, but with room to learn slowly and keep my income. The longer date does not make the basic risk disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you learn from an observation day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d listen to how a support worker explains a missed appointment without blaming the patient. That is a skill I do not learn by writing another check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another city for that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written paid offer that covers the extra rent. There are some developer jobs nearby, so I would look locally first while I still have this wage.

say: I want **workers and clinics** to agree on how appointment mistakes are reported.
I think a **decade** gives our booking team time to fix problems and prepare.
think: I could be **37 in 2036** with software no longer covering rent.
I know **patient-facing work** may also change when robots arrive around 2039.
do: **Keep my developer role** while asking for funded clinic observation days.
**Attend approved days** and save toward six months of bills, then seek paid support work if it survives.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to learn while keeping wages.
S4.quote: Software might no longer buy my rent by 2036.
fieldNote: She treats the decade as time for **funded observation**, not a guarantee of safe work.
Her willingness to move depends on a **written paid offer** covering higher rent.

steps.text: Keep leading the appointment software team while employed
Attend funded quarterly clinic observation days if approved
Save toward six months of bills if wages continue
Seek paid appointment support work if it remains after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our screen work changes before I can test a paid route into clinic support. A funded transition with notice, wages during training and a real support vacancy would help me and the rest of the team.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who answers when a patient misses care because the booking system gave the wrong day. I want the company to name a person for that, even when software writes the code.

headlineQuote: A promise that there might be work someday would not move me.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree, ordinary pay and four months of expenses saved.
She builds **clinic booking software** and measures its quality by missed visits, not coding speed.
She uses AI **occasionally**, testing a method on known incidents before trusting it.
Her **2028 worry** is job loss before a funded path into clinic support is proven.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her screen work before a funded clinic support path exists.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded transition** with notice, continued wages and an actual paid clinic support opening would help.
